stem: A nurse provides health-promotion teaching about calcium and bone health. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Calcium has little role in adult bone because skeletal mineralization is complete by early adulthood
options.B: Calcium intake should routinely exceed recommended amounts because more calcium consistently prevents fractures in all adults
options.C: Adequate vitamin D and physical activity make calcium intake unnecessary for bone maintenance
options.D: Calcium is a major structural component of bone, and intake should generally meet age- and sex-appropriate recommendations

rationale: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements guidance states that calcium makes up much of the structure of bones and that bone undergoes continuous remodeling throughout life. Recommended calcium intake varies by age and sex; for adults, recommended amounts are based largely on bone maintenance and calcium balance. Routine intake above recommended amounts is not supported as a universal fracture-prevention strategy and can carry risks. D is correct.
educational_objective: Explain calcium's ongoing role in bone structure and maintenance and the importance of meeting age-appropriate recommended intake rather than routinely exceeding it.
source_organization: National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements (NIH ODS)

source_original.stem: A nurse provides health-promotion teaching about calcium and bone health. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Calcium has little physiologic role in adult bone because skeletal mineralization is essentially complete once a person reaches early adulthood.
options.B: Calcium supplements should routinely exceed the recommended intake because higher doses consistently provide greater fracture prevention for all adults.
options.C: Vitamin D and physical activity make dietary calcium unnecessary, because bone mineral can be maintained without an adequate calcium supply.
options.D: Adequate calcium is needed for normal bone mineralization and maintenance, while intake should generally meet age-appropriate recommendations.

source_original.rationale: Calcium is a major structural component of bone and adequate intake supports normal bone mineralization and maintenance. Recommended intake varies by age and life stage; routinely exceeding recommended amounts is not a substitute for individualized nutrition and bone-health assessment.
source_original.source_detail: NIH ODS Calcium fact sheet, Health Effects/Bone health section: calcium is central to bone structure; low intake contributes to osteoporosis risk, while supplementation outcomes depend on context. Current NIH ODS fact sheet reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the correct calcium/bone-health concept, tightened the answer to the NIH-supported age- and sex-specific intake framework, and removed the broader claim that supplementation consistently prevents fractures. Exact NIH ODS sections are now identified.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current NIH ODS professional fact sheet; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: NIH ODS Calcium Health Professional fact sheet was opened and reviewed on 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: NIH ODS directly supports calcium's structural role, lifelong bone remodeling, and age/sex-specific recommended intakes based on bone maintenance/balance.

distractor_audit.A: Contradicted by continuous bone remodeling and calcium's structural role.
distractor_audit.B: Overstates benefit and ignores intake limits/context.
distractor_audit.C: Vitamin D supports calcium absorption but does not make calcium intake unnecessary.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: D is uniquely accurate and avoids prescribing supplements when dietary adequacy may suffice.
audit_findings.cueing: Choices are parallel health-teaching statements without answer-length cueing.
audit_findings.blueprint: Preventive nutrition and bone-health education fit Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NIH ODS Introduction and Recommended Intakes; D remains uniquely correct.
